# **Beyond Detection Engineering: Building Security Engineering at Scale**


[Global Technology](https://medium.com/@global_technology?source=post_page---byline--360451a03222-----------------------------------------)


7 min read


·


Just now


--


Detection engineering starts with alerts, but at enterprise scale, success depends on the systems, processes, and engineering discipline behind them.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*By: Matt Clemons, Sr. Manager, Cyber Defense*


**Quick Bytes**


- At enterprise scale, the biggest challenge isn’t writing detections but managing the complexity that comes with growth
- The breakthrough came when detection engineering shifted from creating alerts to building systems that could scale and adapt
- By focusing on telemetry, ownership, and engineering discipline, the team built a stronger foundation for cybersecurity at McDonald’s


Twenty years ago, I thought detection engineering was just about writing rules. Those skills still matter, but after two decades building and scaling detection programs, I’ve learned they are only part of the job.


At McDonald’s, the problem wasn’t that we lacked detections. The problem was that every improvement created additional operational overhead somewhere else in the system. More telemetry produced more alerts. More tuning exposed gaps in telemetry. Every improvement uncovered the next bottleneck.


That’s when it became clear that detection engineering wasn’t just about detections. It was about building a system that could absorb change without depending on constant reactive intervention.


**Scale changes everything** When I joined McDonald’s, the first few months were familiar. Bring in logs, write detections, improve coverage. Repeat. But as the organization grew, so did everything around it. New markets came online. Cloud adoption accelerated. Identity systems expanded. What seemed like incremental growth at McDonald’s translated into millions of authentication events, thousands of connected applications, and an increasingly complex attack surface. Security tooling multiplied. More telemetry sources became available. Other teams needed coverage for new threats. We were no longer managing a small detection backlog. We were managing dozens of telemetry sources across identity, endpoint, cloud, network, and application platforms.


For a while, we responded the way most teams do. We worked harder, added more detections, onboarded more data, and solved problems as they appeared. That approach worked until the complexity outgrew it.


The moment that changed my thinking wasn’t tied to a single detection or incident. Work was coming from email, chat, word of mouth, and informal requests. We could not track demand, measure progress, or explain capacity.


**From detections to engineering** Once we accepted that scale was the problem, it became clear that adding more detections wasn’t the answer. We needed to evolve our operating model.


We formalized our intake procedure, implemented a metrics database, and started planning for the future.


We built a formal detection lifecycle that defined how detections moved from idea to production. Every detection required an owner, documented requirements, validation, peer review, user acceptance testing, promotion criteria, and a plan for long-term maintenance. A detection was no longer complete because the logic looked correct. It was complete only when it could operate reliably in production and someone was accountable for its success over time.


Governance followed naturally. We standardized metadata, ATT&CK mapping, documentation, review criteria, and operational procedures. None of these changes generated a single alert, but they made the entire program more predictable.


Instead of relying on individual engineers to remember how something should be done, we built a system that made the right approach the default. That consistency made it easier to scale, onboard new engineers, and support a rapidly growing global technology environment. It also allowed us to change something more important: the team.


When I joined, much of the work was transactional. Engineers picked up tickets, built detections, tuned alerts, and moved on to the next request. The problem with that is that ticket ownership doesn’t create program ownership. Over time, we started changing the conversations.


Instead of asking, “Who’s writing this detection?” we started asking, “Who’s the owner of this problem?” That subtle shift changed how engineers approached their work.


Engineers who had once focused almost exclusively on execution began driving design discussions, questioning assumptions, identifying systemic problems, and proposing improvements that extended far beyond the original request.


Over time, knowledge stopped living only in people’s heads. The practices that had once depended on individual experience became standards, documentation, automation, and repeatable processes. New engineers had a much lower barrier to entry because the system itself captured what the team had learned.


Looking back, that may have been the most important transformation of all. The success of a detection engineering program should never depend on remembering which person knows the answer. It should depend on building a team, and a system where the answer already exists.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**Owning the signal pipeline** Supporting a global environment meant working with infrastructure teams, cloud engineers, identity teams, regional security owners, and application owners. Every new telemetry source required planning before it was connected. Who owns it? Is the data complete and normalized? Can we trust it? What will it cost? Who monitors its health? Is it valuable enough to justify that support model? Those questions became just as important as the detection logic itself.


Collecting telemetry is the beginning. Data quality, parsing, products, teams, and business requirements all evolve over time.


Early automation efforts focused on reducing repetitive work for analysts. Over time, our thinking shifted. Instead of automating individual tasks, we started looking for opportunities to improve how information moved through the entire system. Enrichment, orchestration, case management, and operational workflows all became part of the same engineering problem.


Detection Engineering was no longer responsible for the alerts coming out of the pipeline. It was responsible for the quality of the pipeline itself. That distinction mattered because scalable organizations are built on reliable systems, not individual outputs. By improving the pipeline, the team created a capability that could support continued growth without requiring effort to scale at the same rate.


A perfectly written detection operating against incomplete, inconsistent, or poorly understood telemetry will never outperform an average detection built on a healthy, well-managed pipeline.


Engineering the pipeline became just as important as engineering the detections.


**The false positive trap** Like most growing security programs, we initially approached false positives the way the industry often does. A detection generated too much noise, we tuned the rule (or turned it off), reduced the alert volume, and moved on to the next problem.


But that’s just treating the symptoms. As we spent more time analyzing our detections, a pattern started to emerge. The noisiest detections were rarely the worst detections. Most were behaving exactly as they had been designed.


Some detections were operating against incomplete telemetry. Others depended on fields that weren’t consistently populated. Some suffered from inconsistent normalization across data sources. Others lacked context needed to distinguish legitimate activity from malicious behavior.


Now we work to provide a full evidence picture. The SIEM is only as good as the data in it and if an analyst must pivot to multiple solutions to tell the story, a detection is incomplete. But this is sure to happen at this scale. Analysts feed us gaps that we cover to continuously improve visibility and detections.


False positives are rarely a tuning problem. They’re a telemetry, governance, validation, or process problem that happens to surface inside a detection. **** For example, what initially appears to be a noisy alert may actually be the result of inconsistent log fields between systems, missing enrichment data, or an onboarding process that never defined how the telemetry should be normalized in the first place. Once you start fixing those upstream problems instead of compensating for them downstream, everything else becomes easier.


**AI changed the speed, not the job** When AI first became widely available, we started experimenting with it to summarize investigations, explain attack techniques, generate detection ideas, write queries, and answer questions faster than a human could.


The technology is impressive, but it’s also easy to overestimate what it can accomplish on its own. AI is only as useful as the engineering foundation around it. If the data isn’t normalized or the documentation doesn’t exist, the model has little context to work from. Instead of asking, “What can AI do?” we started asking, “What engineering work can AI help us do faster?”


It became another engineering tool. It accelerated research, helped analyze coverage, identified gaps, and assisted with drafting detections that the team could make production ready.


Many organizations expected AI to create maturity. It does not. Without consistent telemetry, governance, validation, and engineering discipline, AI simply helps organizations move faster in the wrong direction.


AI didn’t change the job. It changed how much of the job we could spend doing the work that matters most.


**Building confidence at scale** When an incident occurs, the goal is not simply to generate an alert. The goal is to explain what happened, how it happened, what was affected, and what’s next.


Detection engineering is often described as a technical discipline centered on writing rules. In reality, it’s an engineering discipline centered on building confidence. Confidence in the telemetry we collect. Confidence in the detections we deploy. Confidence in the automation we build. Confidence in the people operating the system.


Our responsibility is to build systems that help defenders understand what happened, trust what they are seeing, and make good decisions quickly when it matters most. For a company operating at McDonald’s scale, that means designing capabilities that can grow with the business while remaining consistent, resilient, and trusted wherever they are used.
